description: Team DeHa Space is a group of high-school students and a teacher mentor from Türkiye. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 we built Mission Architect, a bilingual (Turkish/English) 3D browser game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players design a Moon or Mars mission, launch it, fix a failure in orbit, run a surface base and bring the crew home, learning real trade-offs with NASA data along the way.
summary: Mission Architect is a free, browser-based 3D game in which students design, fly and complete a whole crewed mission to the Moon or Mars. Players walk a launch site, then use 8 design stations to choose the destination, science goal, instruments, power, communications, crew, rocket and orbit, while a live bar tracks budget, mass, power and data. After launch the mission continues through 5 chapters: a CO2 failure in orbit fixed with items on board, a player-controlled landing, a surface base with 10 tasks (crew health, greenhouse, solar power, crater, radiation, physics, farm and more) and a return to Earth with the rocket equation, an entry corridor and parachutes. Every choice comes back later, so players see how science, engineering, cost and crew health trade off. Values come from NASA sources such as the Planetary Fact Sheets, the Human Research Program, Veggie, Curiosity RAD, MOXIE and Artemis I. The game runs offline from a single file in Turkish and English, so any classroom can use it.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Mission Architect is a 3D web game for the "Space Mission Design Game" challenge. The player becomes the commander of a crewed mission to the Moon or Mars and takes it from the launch pad all the way back to Earth. Instead of learning subsystems one by one, players see how every decision about science, mass, power, budget, communications and crew health affects the rest of the mission. The game has 5 chapters, 2 destinations, 8 design stations and 10 surface tasks, and it is fully playable in Turkish and English.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Launch site: The player walks to the launch tower, rides the elevator, crosses the crew access arm into the white room and boards the vehicle. Info points explain parts of a real launch complex, such as the sound suppression system and the white room.

2. Mission design: Inside the vehicle, 8 stations set the destination, science goal, instruments, power system, communications, crew, rocket and orbit, and give the final command. Every option shows its mass, power, cost, data and science value. A live bar tracks the limits, and each station ends with a short quiz.

3. Launch and report: The mission launches and a report shows the success probability (mass and power margins, backup antenna, radiation and dust risk), the science score (instruments that fit the goal count fully, others count half) and a grade normalised per destination. The player can redesign and fly again.

4. Failure in orbit: Above the atmosphere a power bus fails and cabin CO2 rises. The player diagnoses the fault, collects floating items, swaps a fuse and builds a CO2 adapter from items on board (inspired by Apollo 13). The player then sends a message to Earth and learns about signal delay (about 1.3 s to the Moon, 3-22 minutes to Mars).

5. Landing: The player flies the lander with the main engine and side thrusters, watching altitude, vertical speed, fuel and distance to the target. On Mars a parachute opens first; on the Moon there is no air, so landing is engine only.

6. Surface base: Every crew member gets a physical and a psychological test. Mental health below 50% leads to sessions with a psychologist; physical problems lead to a diet plan (calories, protein, calcium, vitamin D) and an exercise plan. The base tasks are a greenhouse (light colour, hours, growing medium, water, temperature), solar panels, exploration, a crater study, radiation measurement and a physics lab. Correct physics answers earn an animal from the base farm, whose habitat the player must set up.

7. Return to Earth: The player picks cargo within a mass limit (30 kg from the Moon, 15 kg from Mars), computes ascent fuel with the rocket equation and chooses a return window. During re-entry the player picks an entry angle inside the corridor, keeps the heat shield forward through the radio blackout, opens drogue (5.5-8.5 km) and main (2-4 km) parachutes and splashes down. The crew then goes through a 45-day rehabilitation programme, and a final mission report gives up to 3 stars.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Mission Architect turns systems engineering into something students can feel: raising one value visibly lowers another, and a decision made in chapter 1 matters in chapter 5. It also covers topics that are rarely taught together, including the rocket equation, signal delay, entry corridors, radiation dose, plant growth in space, and the physical and mental health of astronauts. Because it runs offline from a single file, has low/medium/high graphics settings and is bilingual, it can be used in classrooms with limited internet or older computers. Failures are explained, not just punished, so students can retry and learn from mistakes.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

The game is written in JavaScript with Three.js 0.169 (WebGL) and bundled into a single file with esbuild, so it opens by double-clicking index.html with no installation or server. All 3D models, textures and sound effects are generated by code (procedural geometry, canvas textures and the Web Audio API); no external 3D models, images or sound files are used. The interface uses the open-source fonts Exo 2, Rajdhani and Share Tech Mono (SIL Open Font License). Automated playtests and screenshots were made in a headless Chromium browser with Playwright.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Instead of a single design screen, we built a continuous story in which the design is tested by events, so trade-offs have consequences. We based numbers on NASA sources (planetary data, human spaceflight hazards, Veggie, Curiosity RAD, MOXIE, Artemis I, Apollo) and marked values rounded for game balance as "approximate". We balanced difficulty so both destinations are fair (the grade is normalised by destination) and so that "take every instrument" is not a winning strategy. We also considered accessibility for schools: offline use, two languages, adjustable graphics quality, clear goals on screen and a Knowledge Bank that collects every fact the player learns.

USE OF AI

We used Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, to help write and debug the game code, run automated tests, look up and check NASA reference values, write the bilingual (Turkish/English) game text and draft the presentation slides and speaker notes. The team and our teacher mentor wrote the mission scenarios, decided what each chapter should teach, playtested the game and reviewed all content. The 3D scenes and screenshots in the game are rendered by code, not generated as AI images.
